intro: Almost every exam scenario is a variation on one loop. Learn this once and most "what happens next" questions become mechanical instead of memorized.

actors.name: User / Entry Point
actors.role: Where a task originates — a person typing a message, a webhook firing, a cron job kicking off a batch run. The exam treats all three the same: something outside the loop hands the harness a task.

actors.name: The Harness
actors.role: Deterministic code you control: assembles context, calls the API, parses the response, executes tools, enforces gates (budgets, permissions, business rules), and decides whether to loop again or stop. Everything non-negotiable belongs here, not in a prompt.

actors.name: The Model (Claude)
actors.role: The reasoning engine. It reads context and tool definitions and returns a decision as structured data — text, a tool_use block, or both. It never directly touches a database, a file, or a payment rail.

actors.name: Claude API
actors.role: The Messages endpoint the harness calls. It's the boundary between your code and the model — request in (messages, tools, system prompt), response out (content blocks, stop_reason).

actors.name: Tool Backends
actors.role: The real systems a tool call ultimately reaches — a database, an internal API, a payment processor, the filesystem. The model decides to call a tool; the harness's tool-execution code is what actually reaches the backend.

loop_steps.title: Context assembly
loop_steps.detail: The harness gathers what the model needs to decide: conversation history, retrieved documents, prior tool results, system prompt, and the list of tools currently available.

loop_steps.title: Request to the model
loop_steps.detail: The harness sends messages + tool schemas + system prompt to the Claude API. Nothing here is optional context — if the model needs it to decide correctly, it must be in this payload.

loop_steps.title: Model returns a decision
loop_steps.detail: The response comes back with a stop_reason. `end_turn` means Claude is done and produced a final answer. `tool_use` means Claude is requesting one or more tool calls, each as a structured object with a name and input — a decision, not an action.

loop_steps.title: Harness branches on stop_reason
loop_steps.detail: This is where deterministic code takes over. `end_turn` → return the response to the user. `tool_use` → proceed to gate enforcement before anything executes.

loop_steps.title: Gate enforcement
loop_steps.detail: Before a requested tool call actually runs, the harness checks it against hard rules: spend limits, permission scopes, allow/deny lists, rate limits, compliance constraints. A gate is a code-level `if`, not a sentence in the system prompt — no prompt wording lets the model talk its way past one.

loop_steps.title: Tool execution
loop_steps.detail: If the gate passes, the harness's tool-execution code calls the real backend (the actual database write, the actual API request) and captures the result — success, data, or a structured error.

loop_steps.title: Result fed back, loop continues
loop_steps.detail: The tool result is appended to the conversation as a tool_result block and the harness returns to Step 2 — back to the model — until it eventually returns `end_turn` or an explicit exit condition (max turns, escalation) is hit.

loop_steps.title: Verification / evaluation (optional but common on the exam)
loop_steps.detail: Mature harnesses add a check after the loop settles — a schema validator, a second model call acting as a judge, or a human-in-the-loop review — before treating the result as final, especially for high-stakes actions.

core_principle: The model decides; the harness executes. Claude's job ends at returning a structured decision. Whether that decision is allowed to become a real-world effect is entirely the harness's call — which is exactly why guardrails belong in code, not prompt wording.
exam_tip: When a scenario asks "why did the agent do X" or "what should have prevented X," first identify which of the 8 loop steps is being described, then ask whether the failure is a context problem (steps 1-2), a model reasoning problem (step 3), or a missing/weak gate (step 5). The large majority of "design a safer system" questions are really asking you to add or fix a gate at step 5.
